A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same underlying quantization work despite substantial retitling and refocusing. The complete documents, including v3's Appendices A–C and v4's Appendices A–E, provide readable text, equations, figures and experimental evidence.

before.justification: V3 reports original synthetic experiments and classification results on flow cytometry and satellite images, including additional results in Appendix C.

after.justification: V4 reports original Gaussian convergence experiments, a rare-population simulation, and classification and runtime results on flow cytometry and satellite images.

M1.justification: Shared-support quantization, measure-specific Voronoi weights, Lloyd/k-means++ optimization, optional mean-measure subsampling and barycentric LOT construction are already documented in v3 and retained in v4. Individual quantization remains as IQ and in Appendix B; the changed emphasis does not introduce a new algorithm.

E1.justification: V4 replaces the compact-reference shift-and-scaling experiment with Gaussian studies that evaluate barycenter, dispersion and covariance approximation, and adds normal/rare/absent-population scenarios. The cytometry and Airbus datasets remain, but hospital-of-origin classification is removed; hospital labels still appear in PCA visualizations.

E2.justification: V4 removes Nyström KME and random-subset-plus-KME comparisons from both real datasets, and RFF from cytometry. It adds the uniform-weight empirical-subsampling baseline Emp. IQ and the Voronoi-weighted random-subset comparator are retained under new names, while full and subsampled MMQ receive separate comparisons.

E3.justification: Real-data classification changes from LDA after 10-component PCA with a 75/25 split to LDA on LOT embeddings with stratified 67/33 splits. Reference-measure sample sizes change from 1,000 to 100. The classification K grid changes from 16, 32, 64 and 128 to 10, 30, 50, 70, 100, 150 and 200.

E4.justification: V4 adds a rare-population case study testing how shared atoms represent disappearing components and explicitly compares full versus subsampled MMQ. Gaussian barycenter, dispersion and covariance convergence analyses replace the earlier synthetic Gram-error, PCA and sample-size runtime analyses. Real-data sensitivity to K is also re-evaluated.

E5.justification: V3's classification tables give point estimates; Figure 4 contains shaded bands without explaining them or specifying a run count. V4 specifies 20 independent trials with 95% confidence intervals for Figure 1, and classification means and standard deviations over 30 stratified random splits for both real datasets.

E6.justification: V3 Table 1 reports 94% versus 81% cytometry-type accuracy for MMQ versus individual quantization at K=64. V4's replacement results generally place IQ highest, with MMQ close behind (Figures 3 and 6), under substantially different settings that prevent direct performance comparisons. Gaussian convergence and rare-population findings are added, while hospital-classification, KME and earlier synthetic results are removed.

T1.justification: V4 introduces covariance-operator bounds for bounded Hölder embeddings, with LOT and KME specializations (Proposition 4.4 and Appendix D), and rederives the Gram bound in Appendix E. V3's empirical-estimation Theorem 3.9, explicit PCA excess-risk Proposition 4.7 and synthetic Gram-formula derivations are removed. Core quantization, barycenter, dispersion and clustering results remain, including individual-quantization consistency in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift from two quantization approaches for LOT and KME embeddings to shared-support MMQ for OT-based learning. Individual quantization becomes the principal baseline, while shared-support storage and interpretability benefits become central to the motivation. The fundamental consistency and computational-efficiency claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 adds a substantive explanation of how aligned atoms and vanishing weights reveal rare or absent populations. It recasts the real-data interpretation from MMQ's superior or similar accuracy to a tradeoff in which IQ generally performs best and subsampled MMQ approaches its accuracy at lower cost. The curse-of-dimensionality limitation is retained.

D1.justification: V4 adds explicit empirical-mean construction and sampling details for the new synthetic experiments, and revises computational-cost expressions. KME-specific implementation details and the explicit POT solver reference disappear. Lloyd/k-means++, the mean-subsampling rule and barycentric projection were already documented in v3.

R1.justification: Research positioning narrows from broad Hilbert-space embedding and KME approximation to shared-support OT learning. V4 removes the Nyström discussion and the broad novelty assertion about simultaneous quantization for scalable embeddings, while adding pooled-clustering and rare-cell positioning through SWIFT and a computational-barycenter reference. Many distribution-regression and kernel-method references are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. LOT background moves into Section 4.4, individual quantization moves largely to Appendix B, and the appendices are reorganized around separate proof topics. These are substantial narrative changes beyond the accompanying scientific additions and removals.

P2.justification: V3's eight classification tables are replaced by accuracy/runtime plots. V4 introduces Gaussian convergence and rare-population figures, removes the earlier schematic and synthetic PCA/Gram displays, and redraws the cytometry PCA comparison. The identical satellite-image examples move from v3's appendix Figure 8 to v4's main-text Figure 5.

improvement.justification: V4 better supports the central accuracy–cost tradeoff through explicit full/subsampled comparisons, classification summaries over 30 stratified splits, and clearly defined uncertainty reporting. The Gaussian and rare-population studies also clarify the evidence and shared-support benefits. These gains are moderated by the loss of finite-sample and explicit PCA guarantees and reduced comparison coverage, yielding a limited net improvement.
